column.text: The Lamplighter's Almanac

The lamp-keepers of the northern coast kept a record of every evening they lit the harbor, and the record grew longer than the harbor itself. Most nights the third column stayed empty, and the keepers took pride in that, since a quiet night meant a safe one. The oldest keeper claimed that she could tell the season from the smell of the oil alone, and she was seldom wrong. Nobody could say when the first entry was made, only that the ink in it had faded to the color of weak tea.

Nobody could say when the first entry was made, only that the ink in it had faded to the color of weak tea. When a storm did come, the entries ran past the margin and onto the back of the page, written in a hurried hand. Under the lamp room stood a cupboard of spare wicks, glass chimneys and one brass bell that nobody remembered buying. A page of the record was ruled into three columns: the hour, the weather, and a line for anything worth remembering.
